I want to tell you about the sound the refrigerator makes at 3:17 a.m.

It’s not a hum. It’s a sigh. A long, low exhale that happens every twenty-seven minutes, like clockwork, like it’s breathing in time with a city it will never see. I only know this because I am awake. I shouldn’t be awake. The apartment is dark except for the blue bar of light from the microwave clock and the little red dot on the router that blinks like it’s winking at me. My phone is on the nightstand, face down, and I have been staring at the ceiling for so long that the cracks in the plaster have started to look like a map.

I came here to write something, anything, for a thousand words. That’s the assignment. Write freely about whatever you want. Which is a funny kind of freedom, because freedom usually comes with a little anxiety attached. When you are told to write about nothing in particular, you suddenly become very aware of everything in particular. The refrigerator. The radiator ticking. The way my socks feel a little damp because I forgot to take them off before bed.

There is a mug on the kitchen counter that I used this morning. It’s chipped on the rim and the inside is stained with old tea. I keep meaning to throw it out and I never do. It has become a kind of landmark. If the mug is there, the day has started. If it’s in the sink, the day is over. Right now it’s there, and the day hasn’t started yet, which means I am in between.

I think about how strange it is that we build our lives around these small, repeatable observations. We tell ourselves stories to make the repetition bearable. The refrigerator sighs, so I am not alone. The radiator ticks, so the building is alive. The red dot blinks, so someone, somewhere, is still listening.

When I was a kid, my grandmother kept a notebook by her bed. Not a diary, exactly. She would write down the things she saw out the window. “Sparrow on the fire escape, 7:04.” “Truck with a ladder, blue.” “Mrs. Alvarez arguing with her son again.” She said it helped her remember that she was paying attention. She died with thirty-seven notebooks filled with these tiny observations. No one ever read them. I found them in a box after the funeral and I read one. It made me cry, not because it was sad, but because it was so honest. She wasn’t trying to be profound. She was just trying to be present.

That’s what this feels like now. Trying to be present with 1000 words.

I could write about work. I could write about the email I didn’t send, the one that sat in my drafts for three days. It said thank you. It said I’m sorry. It said I miss you. I never sent it because I was afraid that saying it would make it less true, or more true than I could handle. Instead I wrote a to-do list and called it productivity.

I could write about love. About how it’s easier to love an idea of a person than the actual person who leaves wet towels on the floor and forgets to text back. About how the best moments are usually the ones you don’t plan to keep. The laugh in the car at a red light. The way someone’s hand fits into yours when you’re both too cold to feel it properly.

I could write about the internet. About how we are all sitting in our separate kitchens at 3 a.m., typing into the void, hoping someone on the other side will understand the specific sound our refrigerator makes. About how loneliness has become a kind of collective experience. We are lonely together. We comment, we like, we send heart emojis, and for a second the red dot feels less like a wink and more like a heartbeat.

I could write about death. About the way my grandmother’s notebooks made me think about what we leave behind. Not the big things. The wills and the photos and the carefully curated obituaries. The small things. A chipped mug. A sighing refrigerator. A list of sparrows. Maybe that’s all any of us really leaves. Evidence that we were paying attention for a little while.

I could write about writing. About how it always starts with an excuse. I’m not a writer. I don’t know what I’m doing. The words are not good enough. And then you write one sentence, and then another, and suddenly you’re not thinking about whether it’s good, you’re just trying to keep up with the thoughts that keep coming. That’s the trick. You don’t find the story. The story finds you when you stop trying to control it.

It’s 3:29 now. The refrigerator sighed again. I got up to get water and I saw my reflection in the dark window above the sink. I look tired. I look a little bit relieved. The mug is still there. The day hasn’t started yet.

I think I’ll keep writing. Not because I have to hit a word count, but because there is something comforting about turning the noise of the night into sentences. The radiator ticks, the router blinks, the refrigerator sighs, and I am here, translating it all into words I can hold for a minute before they disappear.

If you ever find yourself awake at 3 a.m., listen. The house is talking to you. It’s telling you small, boring, beautiful things. Write them down. Not because they matter to anyone else, but because they mattered to you for one moment when you were paying attention.

I’m going to turn off the light now. The clock will keep going. The refrigerator will sigh again in about eight minutes. And somewhere, in some other apartment, someone else is probably writing about it too.
